claim: AI-assisted legacy codebase understanding should explicitly run as an investigation phase before any refactor prompt, instructing the model 'Analyze this function without changing it... Do not propose a refactor yet,' because premature refactor suggestions bypass the business-logic context (e.g., magic thresholds, country-specific payment rules) a surface-level code read cannot reveal.
stance_target: codebase mastery requires an investigation-first agent sequence rather than direct code-modification prompting
scope_conditions: legacy codebase modernization/refactoring workflows using AI coding assistants
quoted_support: Analyze this function without changing it. Identify: 1. explicit business rules, 2. likely business rules that need confirmation... Do not propose a refactor yet. ... You want the model in investigation mode, not solution mode.

claim: Legacy business objects frequently have multiple undocumented entry points beyond the obvious API endpoint (background workers, scheduled jobs, migration scripts, webhooks), and analyzing only controllers can miss half of a system's actual entry surface.
stance_target: codebase mastery must map all entry points, not just HTTP-visible ones, before dependency/blast-radius analysis
quoted_support: Web applications often have an obvious HTTP entry point. But legacy systems frequently have several more... If you only analyze controllers, you may miss half the system.

claim: Refactoring a function while preserving only its documented return value can silently break production behavior, because functions often carry hidden side effects (cache invalidation, event emission, email sends, audit writes) that are not visible from the function's name or signature.
stance_target: automated code-blast-radius assessment must trace side effects, not just data flow/return types
quoted_support: If you refactor the function and preserve only its return value, you can break production behavior without any compiler error.

claim: Idempotency gaps are a concrete, named risk class in legacy systems: a worker that charges a card then marks an order paid in two separate steps can double-charge a customer if it crashes between the steps and retries, a failure mode invisible from the function name alone.
stance_target: retry/idempotency analysis is a required part of automated codebase risk mapping
quoted_support: Suppose a worker does this: await chargeCard(order); await markOrderAsPaid(order); If the worker crashes between those two lines and retries, what happens? You may charge the customer twice. And that's not visible from the function name.

claim: AI-generated dependency maps and architectural claims about a legacy codebase must be independently verified using repository search, test suites, database schema inspection, production logs/telemetry, and git history (git log -S, git blame), because 'AI should accelerate search, not replace it.'
stance_target: AI outputs require a validation hierarchy / human-in-the-loop verification, countering zero-hallucination risk
quoted_support: AI-generated explanations can sound convincing even when they're incomplete. So every important finding should have another source of evidence. I use a simple hierarchy. Repository Search... Tests... Database Schema... Logs and Observability... Version History.

claim: High-level prompts like 'Rewrite this application using Clean Architecture' or 'Convert this monolith into microservices' are anti-patterns for initial legacy analysis because they presuppose a solution before the system's actual requirements have been established.
stance_target: jumping directly to solution-oriented agent prompts before investigation is sound practice
quoted_support: There are several prompts I avoid at the beginning of a legacy modernization project. For example: Rewrite this application using Clean Architecture... The problem isn't that AI can't produce useful output from those prompts. It can. The problem is that those questions already contain a solution.

claim: A well-functioning AI investigation of legacy code should produce explicit statements of uncertainty (e.g., 'I cannot determine why this condition exists from the available code') rather than confident but unverifiable explanations, because uncertainty is itself actionable information for engineers.
stance_target: zero-hallucination quality control values explicit uncertainty over confident fabrication
quoted_support: A confident but incorrect answer is much more dangerous. When working with legacy systems, uncertainty is information. Treat it that way.

claim: Duplicated-looking business rules found by AI across modules should not automatically be assumed to require merging, since the duplication may reflect two domains that evolved independently rather than accidental redundancy.
stance_target: automated duplication detection should trigger automatic consolidation without human judgment
quoted_support: Duplication is sometimes accidental. Sometimes it represents two domains that evolved independently. Don't let an AI assistant turn 'similar' into 'must be merged' without evidence.
